title: How the CPU Executes Instructions
description: Walk through the fetch-decode-execute cycle, understand clock speed, and see how pipelining and branch prediction make modern CPUs blazingly fast.

segments.text: Let's crack open the CPU and see what actually happens when your code runs. Spoiler: it's beautifully mechanical, like a perfectly choreographed assembly line.

At its core, a CPU does one thing over and over: fetch an instruction from memory, decode what it means, and execute it. That's it. Fetch, decode, execute. Every program you've ever run boils down to this cycle.

Fetch: the CPU looks at the program counter, which holds the memory address of the next instruction. It pulls that instruction from memory into the instruction register. Think of it as reading the next line of a recipe.

Decode: the control unit figures out what the instruction means. Is it an add? A load? A jump? Then execute: the ALU or other unit carries out the operation. One instruction done, program counter moves forward.

Now, how fast does this cycle spin? That's your clock speed. A 3 GHz processor ticks three billion times per second. Each tick can push an instruction through a stage. Faster clock, more instructions per second.
But here's the thing. While one instruction executes, the fetch and decode units sit idle. That feels wasteful, doesn't it?
segments.thought_prompt: What if we could keep all three stages busy at the same time?

segments.text: That's exactly what pipelining does. While instruction one executes, instruction two is decoding, and instruction three is being fetched. Like an assembly line in a factory, every stage is always busy.

Without pipelining, three instructions take nine clock cycles. With pipelining, they take just five. The throughput nearly triples. Modern CPUs have fifteen to twenty pipeline stages, squeezing out even more parallelism.
But pipelining has a nemesis: branches. When the code says 'if this, do that,' the CPU doesn't know which instruction comes next until the condition is evaluated. The pipeline stalls, waiting.

Enter branch prediction. The CPU guesses which way the branch will go based on history. If a loop has branched back ninety-nine times, it'll probably branch back again. Modern predictors are right over ninety-seven percent of the time.

When the prediction is wrong, the CPU has to flush the pipeline and start over. That's expensive. It's why sorting an array can sometimes make unrelated code faster, because sorted data has more predictable branches.
segments.thought_prompt: Can you think of code patterns that would confuse a branch predictor?

segments.text: So remember: every instruction goes through fetch, decode, execute. Pipelining keeps the CPU busy. And branch prediction gambles on the future to avoid stalls. These three ideas are why your CPU does billions of operations per second.
